newsitem.title: PERU: Peru rebels free 10 hostages, threaten to kill rest.
newsitem.headline: Peru rebels free 10 hostages, threaten to kill rest.

text.p: Leftist guerrillas, threatening to kill hundreds of hostages in the Japanese ambassador's residence, freed 10 hostages on Wednesday including three ambassadors to mediate the release of the captives in exchange for jailed rebels.

The guerrillas, who stormed the compound on Tuesday, called on Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori to personally negotiate for the release of captives, including the Peruvian foreign and agriculture ministers and at least 12 more ambassadors from Asia, Europe and the Americas.
In Tokyo on Thursday, Japanese Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda left for Lima to help resolve the crisis of the 484 hostages still left in the compound.

"It's a difficult situation, but our prime concern is to see that the hostages are released safely and we will do our best to see that the situation is quickly and peacefully resolved," Ikeda told reporters.

The rebels from the Cuban-inspired Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) told reporters from within the building they had laid explosive booby-traps at the entrances in case police try to storm the compound.

The guerrillas, who are demanding the release of up to 500 jailed rebels, freed the ambassadors from Germany, Canada, Greece, and a cultural attache at the French embassy to start negotiations with the government.

"We have been freed by the (guerrillas) to serve as a contact and bridge with the Peruvian government with the aim of looking for a solution through negotiation that avoids bloodshed," the Canadian Ambassador Anthony Vincent told reporters on his release.
The diplomats met immediately with government mediator Education Minister Domingo Palermo Cabrejos, and promised to maintain contact with the rebels by telephone.
One hour after the three ambassadors were freed, Red Cross officials took into the embassy residence supplies of food, water and an X-ray machine on trolleys.
Peru's largest human rights group said it had received a communication from the hostages warning the health of some was in danger.
But Peruvian cameraman Juan Victor Sumarriba, who was allowed into the residency by the rebels, reported on his exit that the hostages were walking around and talking among themselves freely.
Wednesday's releases followed the freeing Tuesday night of about 80 women and old people, leaving only men captives.
The MRTA rebels said they would kill all remaining hostages unless the government freed their jailed comrades.
"If they do not release our prisoners, we will all die in here," an MRTA guerrilla told a local radio station from within the embassy residence.

Tensions rose dramatically around noon EST (1700 GMT) on Wednesday when the rebels issued an ultimatum that they would kill Peruvian Foreign Minister Francisco Tudela unless Fujimori joined the negotiations.
The threat came after an explosion and gunfire rocked the building but the deadline passed without incident.

"The only solution is a political one," MRTA member Walter Loayza said, adding that the rebels wanted transportation for them and the freed prisoners to a guerrilla-controlled area in the country's jungle.
Fujimori called a second emergency Cabinet meeting for Thursday morning but has so far not commented publicly on the attack.
Guerrilla spokesmen said they attacked the Japanese ambassador's home in protest at Tokyo's support for Fujimori, the son of Japanese immigrants, and his economic policies.

Japan was chosen as a target "due to the constant meddling of the Japanese government in Peru," the rebels said in a message sent with a released hostage, Sally Bowen, the president of Peru's foreign correspondents' association.
Governments around the world urged Peru to do everything in its power to protect the hostages and not use force to flush out the rebels.

Japan, Austria, Spain, South Korea, Panama, Malaysia, Venezuela, Bolivia, Brazil, Cuba, Guatemala and Honduras confirmed their ambassadors were among the hostages. The U.S. ambassador was present at the reception but left before the attack, according to the State Department.

The drama began around 8 p.m EST (0100 GMT) Tuesday when heavily armed rebels attacked the building, firing a rocket from outside, and around 20 rebels swarmed inside after blowing a hole in an outside wall, according to witnesses.
Juan Carlos Mejia, head of the special police task force handling the siege, confirmed the rebels had smuggled ammunition into the residency among flowers and Christmas cake.

Thursday's edition of Peruvian daily La Republica said the rebels entered through a tunnel, and also said President Alberto Fujimori's brother, Pedro, was among the hostages. Neither version could be confirmed immediately.

As well as Tudela, the Peruvian hostages included Agriculture Minister Rodolfo Munante Sanguineti, Supreme Court President Moises Pantoja, the current and past chiefs of Peru's anti-terrorism police, Maximo Rivera and Carlos Dominguez respectively, and at least three legislators.

The rebels said they had 400 to 500 comrades in jail and insisted their highest priority was the release of Victor Polay, their leader who was imprisoned in 1992. They also called for a review of Peru's judicial system.
The attack was a major blow to Fujimori's government, which had claimed virtual victory in a 16-year war on communist rebels belonging to the MRTA and the larger and better-known Maoist Shining Path.
